chunks: Edge rate too slow vs too fast. The question: What happens if signal rising edge is too slow? Too fast?
An edge can be too slow or too fast, and each fails in its own way.
A slow edge lingers near the receiver's switching point, so noise can shift or even repeat the switching moment.
A fast edge causes ringing, crosstalk, ground bounce and radio interference. The goal is the slowest edge that still meets your timing.
Think of a door. A person who hovers in the doorway is neither in nor out. One small nudge decides which, so you cannot tell exactly when they crossed.
That is a slow edge near the threshold. Slamming the door shut settles the question instantly, but it rattles the whole house. That is a fast edge.
A door closed at a firm, steady pace avoids both problems.
The same 200 millivolts peak, 300 megahertz noise is added to both edges.
The fast edge crosses the threshold once, almost vertically, so 200 millivolts of noise can move the crossing by at most about 0. 2 volts / 2. 64 volts/ns about 76 picoseconds.
The slow edge crawls through the threshold region (0. 26 volts/ns), so the same noise can shift the crossing by up to about 0.
76 nanoseconds, and here the noise wiggle stalls it right at the threshold (near 8 nanoseconds), where a little more noise would give several crossings.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from 10% to 90% of its swing. Threshold: the voltage at which the receiver switches, usually about halfway.
Slew rate: how fast the voltage changes, in volts per ns. The edge's slope. Jitter: edges arriving earlier or later than they should ("Jitter").
Ringing: wobbles after an edge, like a struck bell still humming ("Ringing").
A 3. 3 volts signal has a 1 nanoseconds rise time. Its slope is about 2. 64 volts/ns (80% of 3. 3 volts in 1 nanoseconds). Add 20 millivolts of noise right at the threshold.
The edge crossing moves by 20 millivolts / 2. 64 volts/ns, which is about 7. 6 picoseconds. Slow the edge to 10 nanoseconds. The slope falls to 0.
264 volts/ns, and the same 20 millivolts of noise moves the crossing by about 76 picoseconds, ten times more. That is the cost of a slow edge.
That is the whole idea: noise turns into timing error faster when the slope is shallow.
"Too slow, and the edge sits near the threshold: noise turns into timing jitter or even multiple crossings, setup margin shrinks, and CMOS inputs draw shoot-through current.
Too fast, and the line behaves like a transmission line so you get reflections and ringing, more crosstalk, ground bounce from the current spikes, and more EMI.
So I pick the slowest edge that still meets timing, using drive strength, a series resistor or termination."
